newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela seeking direct meeting between Zaire rivals.
newsitem.headline: Mandela seeking direct meeting between Zaire rivals.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela will meet Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila in Cape Town on Wednesday evening in a bid to arrange a meeting between Kabila and ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"The president will meet Mr Kabila this evening to interact and exchange views on the path to take the peace-making process forward," Mandela's spokesman Parks Mankahlana told Reuters.
He confirmed that U.N. envoy Mahomed Sahnoun was in Cape town to assist the process.
A senior source said Mandela wanted to bring Mobutu and Kabila together in South Africa as part of his efforts to bring peace to Zaire.
No definite arrangements had been made for the face-to-face meeting between the two rivals, but the source predicted it could take place by the weekend.
The source said Kabila would meet Mandela at his Cape Town residence, Genadendal.

Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister Aziz Pahad, who was instrumental in arranging an earlier round of talks in South Africa between representatives of the Zairean rivals, was expected to attend Wednesday night's talks.
Kabila arrived in South Africa on Wednesday from Zaire's Lubumbashi airport but there was no word on the movements of the Zairean president.
The source declined any further comment on the talks, saying it would be for the rebels and the Zairean government to make any statements.
Speaking earlier to reporters at Lubumbashi airport, Kabila reasserted that nothing would halt his drive to unseat Mobutu.
"There will be no ceasefire until Mobutu relinquishes power," the rebel leader said.
Kabila, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), had earlier told Reuters by telephone that the "people are against a ceasefire".
"The people do not want a ceasefire, they want an end to this corrupt regime," said Kabila.
Kabila insists on direct talks with Mobutu, who has cancer, to negotiate an end to his 32-year rule.
After crippling Kinshasa with an anti-Mobutu protest action on Monday and Tuesday, Zaire's main opposition called a meeting of its leadership on Wednesday to plan further measures.
"We will launch new measures for the coming week. The action will continue," declared Mukendi wa Kamanda, chief political aide to opposition stalwart Etienne Tshisekedi.

Shops and businesses reopened on Wednesday and the city regained its normal pace after a well-observed stay-at-home protest on Monday. Police thwarted a student protest march on Tuesday but Kinshasa residents stayed at home all the same.

Kabila's rebels who have seized over half of Zaire since taking up arms to topple Mobutu in October, formally resumed their whirlwind drive last weekend after a three-day pause to allow Mobutu time to show a willingness to step down.
The rebels say they are now 300 km (180 miles) from Kinshasa, a claim ridiculed by the Zaire government and questioned by independent military analysts.
But given the inability of Zaire's undisciplined army to offer resistance to the rebels, many Zaireans doubt government forces will be capable of holding Kinshasa.
Kabila's alliance signed on Wednesday a $1 billion deal with America Mineral Fields Inc. it hopes will resurrect the fabled mineral wealth of Shaba province.
